subject: chemistry
subTopic: Electrolysis of Molten and Aqueous Compounds

questions.content: A teacher says: "Electrolysis is used to split some compounds into their elements." Which description of electrolysis is correct?
options: Breaking down an ionic compound using an electric current
Joining two elements using heat
Separating a mixture by boiling
Dissolving a salt in water
questions.explanation: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to decompose an ionic compound that is molten or dissolved in water.

questions.content: A student tests four substances in a circuit with a bulb. Solid sodium chloride does not light the bulb, but molten sodium chloride does. What is the best explanation?
options: Solid sodium chloride has no ions
In the solid the ions cannot move, but in the liquid they can
Electrons flow through molten sodium chloride only
Molten sodium chloride contains atoms instead of ions
questions.explanation: Ionic solids have ions locked in a lattice. When molten (or dissolved) the ions are free to move and carry charge.

questions.content: During electrolysis, positive ions are attracted to which electrode?
options: The anode, because it is positive
The cathode, because it is negative
The anode, because it is negative
The cathode, because it is positive
questions.explanation: Positive ions (cations) move to the negative electrode, the cathode. A memory aid is that cations go to the cathode.

questions.content: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What are the products?
options: Lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Bromine at the cathode and lead at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Lead at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
questions.explanation: Pb²⁺ ions gain electrons at the cathode to form lead metal, and Br⁻ ions lose electrons at the anode to form bromine. There is no water, so no hydrogen or oxygen.

questions.content: What word describes a compound that conducts electricity and is decomposed when molten or dissolved in water?
options: Electrode
Electrolyte
Insulator
Catalyst
questions.explanation: An electrolyte is an ionic compound that conducts when molten or in solution and is broken down by the current.

questions.content: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using inert graphite electrodes. What is formed at each electrode?
options: Copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Copper at the cathode and sulfur at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and sulfur dioxide at the anode
questions.explanation: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen so Cu²⁺ is discharged at the cathode. Sulfate ions are not discharged, so hydroxide ions from water give oxygen at the anode.

questions.content: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (brine) is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which row correctly gives the cathode product, anode product and the substance left in solution?
options: Sodium, chlorine, water
Hydrogen, chlorine, sodium hydroxide solution
Hydrogen, oxygen, sodium chloride solution
Sodium, oxygen, sodium hydroxide solution
questions.explanation: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen so H⁺ ions from water are discharged at the cathode. In concentrated solution chloride is discharged at the anode. Na⁺ and OH⁻ stay behind as sodium hydroxide.

questions.content: Which half-equation shows what happens at the cathode when copper(II) ions are discharged?
options: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻
2Cu²⁺ → Cu + 2e⁻
Cu²⁺ → Cu + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Positive ions gain electrons at the cathode, which is reduction. The electrons appear on the left side of the equation.

questions.content: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed. A student collects 4.0 dm³ of hydrogen at the cathode. What volume of oxygen should collect at the anode, assuming both are measured under the same conditions?
options: 8.0 dm³
4.0 dm³
2.0 dm³
1.0 dm³
questions.explanation: Water splits as 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, so gas volumes are in the ratio 2 : 1. Half of 4.0 dm³ is 2.0 dm³.

questions.content: A gas is produced at the anode during electrolysis of brine. It turns damp blue litmus paper red and then bleaches it white. Which gas is it?
options: Hydrogen
Oxygen
Chlorine
Carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Damp litmus paper bleached white is the test for chlorine. Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop and oxygen relights a glowing splint.

questions.content: Aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite before electrolysis. Why is this done?
options: Cryolite is a catalyst that speeds up the reaction
It lowers the temperature needed to keep the electrolyte molten
Cryolite reacts with oxygen to protect the anode
It makes aluminium oxide less reactive
questions.explanation: Pure aluminium oxide melts at above 2000 °C. Dissolving it in cryolite gives a mixture that is molten at a much lower temperature, saving energy and cost.

questions.content: Which half-equation represents oxidation at the anode when chloride ions are discharged?
options: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
Cl⁻ + e⁻ → Cl
2Cl⁻ + 2e⁻ → Cl₂
questions.explanation: At the anode, ions lose electrons (oxidation). Two chloride ions each lose one electron, so the electrons are on the right side and the atoms balance as Cl₂.

questions.content: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes for 30 minutes. The blue colour of the solution gets paler. What is the best explanation?
options: Water is being produced and dilutes the solution
Copper(II) ions are being removed as copper metal
Sulfate ions are being converted to oxygen
The electrodes are dissolving into the solution
questions.explanation: The blue colour is due to Cu²⁺ ions. They are discharged as copper at the cathode, so their concentration falls and the colour fades.

questions.content: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. A dilute solution gives oxygen at the anode, but a concentrated solution gives chlorine. What does this show?
options: Oxygen is always more reactive than chlorine
Chloride ions are discharged in preference to hydroxide ions only when their concentration is high enough
Dilute solutions contain no chloride ions
Chlorine cannot form in water
questions.explanation: In a dilute solution there are few Cl⁻ ions, so OH⁻ ions from water are discharged to give oxygen. A high concentration of Cl⁻ makes chlorine the main product.

questions.content: Aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) is electrolysed to make aluminium. The relative formula mass of Al₂O₃ is 102 and the relative atomic mass of aluminium is 27. What mass of aluminium can be made from 204 tonnes of pure aluminium oxide, assuming complete conversion?
options: 54 tonnes
108 tonnes
204 tonnes
216 tonnes
questions.explanation: 204 t is 2 × 102, so there are 2 formula units' worth. Each Al₂O₃ contains 54 of aluminium, so the mass is 2 × 54 = 108 tonnes. Choosing 54 forgets to scale for 204 t.

questions.content: Potassium iodide is electrolysed in two ways: first as a molten liquid, then as an aqueous solution, using inert electrodes. Which row gives the cathode product in each case?
options: Molten: potassium; aqueous: hydrogen
Molten: hydrogen; aqueous: potassium
Molten: potassium; aqueous: potassium
Molten: iodine; aqueous: hydrogen
questions.explanation: Molten KI contains only K⁺ and I⁻, so potassium forms at the cathode. In solution, water supplies H⁺ and potassium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen is produced.

questions.content: A student electrolyses water and collects 24 cm³ of hydrogen. The oxygen collected is 11 cm³. The theoretical volume of oxygen is 12 cm³. What is the percentage error in the oxygen volume, and which factor best explains the gap?
options: 8.3%; oxygen is slightly more soluble in water than hydrogen
8.3%; hydrogen is more soluble than oxygen
4.2%; oxygen is lost when the circuit is switched off
9.1%; the ratio of gases should be 1 : 1
questions.explanation: The difference is 1 cm³ out of 12 cm³, which is 8.3%. Oxygen dissolves in water a little more than hydrogen, and it can also react with the electrodes, so less is collected. The ratio is 2 : 1, not 1 : 1.

questions.content: A student predicts the products of electrolysing aqueous silver nitrate with inert electrodes. Which prediction is correct and has the correct reasoning?
options: Silver at the cathode, because silver is less reactive than hydrogen; oxygen at the anode, because nitrate ions are not discharged
Hydrogen at the cathode, because water is always discharged first; nitrogen at the anode
Silver at the cathode; nitrogen dioxide at the anode, because nitrate is always discharged
Hydrogen at the cathode; oxygen at the anode, because silver is more reactive than hydrogen
questions.explanation: Silver is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so Ag⁺ is discharged to form silver. Nitrate ions are not discharged in aqueous solution, so hydroxide ions form oxygen at the anode.

note:
## What is electrolysis?
Electrolysis is the breaking down of an ionic compound using electricity. The compound must be an **electrolyte**, which means it is either **molten** (melted) or **dissolved in water**. In both cases the ions are free to move. In a solid ionic compound the ions are locked in a lattice, so a solid does not conduct and cannot be electrolysed.

The circuit has a power supply, two **electrodes** dipped into the electrolyte, and often inert electrodes made of graphite or platinum so that they do not react.
- The **cathode** is the negative electrode. Positive ions (cations) move there and gain electrons. This is **reduction**.
- The **anode** is the positive electrode. Negative ions (anions) move there and lose electrons. This is **oxidation**.

## Molten compounds
When a molten binary compound is electrolysed, the only ions present are the two from the compound, so the products are easy to predict. A metal forms at the cathode and a non-metal forms at the anode.
- Molten lead(II) bromide: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb at the cathode, and 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ at the anode.
- Molten aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite is used to extract aluminium. Cryolite lowers the melting temperature, saving energy. The graphite anodes slowly burn away as oxygen reacts with them, so they must be replaced.

## Aqueous solutions
Water also contains a few H⁺ and OH⁻ ions, so there are two possible ions at each electrode.
- At the cathode, the **less reactive** element is discharged. If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen (for example sodium, potassium, calcium), hydrogen gas forms. If it is less reactive (for example copper, silver), the metal forms.
- At the anode, if a halide ion (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) is present in enough concentration, the halogen forms. Otherwise OH⁻ ions are discharged and oxygen forms: 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻. Sulfate and nitrate ions are not discharged.

Examples: brine (concentrated sodium chloride) gives hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide solution. Copper(II) sulfate solution gives copper and oxygen, and the blue colour fades as Cu²⁺ ions are used up. Dilute sulfuric acid gives hydrogen and oxygen in a 2 : 1 volume ratio.

## Gas tests
- Hydrogen: a lit splint gives a squeaky pop.
- Oxygen: relights a glowing splint.
- Chlorine: bleaches damp litmus paper.

## Worked example
Aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, has a relative formula mass of 102, and 54 of that is aluminium (2 × 27). From 204 tonnes of Al₂O₃ you can make 204 × 54 ÷ 102 = 108 tonnes of aluminium, assuming complete conversion.

## Common mistakes
- Writing that electrons flow through the electrolyte. Electrons flow in the wires; ions carry charge in the liquid.
- Mixing up which electrode is positive. Cations go to the cathode.
- Forgetting that water takes part in aqueous electrolysis.
- Putting electrons on the wrong side of a half-equation. At the cathode they are on the left, at the anode on the right.

## How this is examined
In eAssessment-style questions you are usually given a context such as a chlor-alkali plant or a lab investigation with a table of results. You may be asked to state the products, write half-equations, explain why hydrogen forms instead of a reactive metal, calculate a mass or gas volume, and evaluate the accuracy of an experiment by finding a percentage error and commenting on limitations such as gas solubility.

Exam tip: Always name the electrode and say which ion is discharged and why, using the reactivity series for the cathode and the concentration of halide ions for the anode.

flashcards.front: Define electrolysis.
flashcards.back: The breaking down of an ionic compound, when molten or dissolved in water, using an electric current.

flashcards.front: Why must an electrolyte be molten or dissolved?
flashcards.back: The ions must be free to move to the electrodes. In a solid ionic lattice the ions are fixed in place.

flashcards.front: Cathode or anode: which is negative, and what happens there?
flashcards.back: The cathode is negative. Positive ions gain electrons there (reduction).

flashcards.front: Anode: charge and process?
flashcards.back: The anode is positive. Negative ions lose electrons there (oxidation).

flashcards.front: Rule for the cathode product in aqueous electrolysis
flashcards.back: The less reactive element is discharged. Metals below hydrogen (Cu, Ag) form metal; reactive metals (Na, K) give hydrogen.

flashcards.front: Rule for the anode product in aqueous electrolysis
flashcards.back: Halide ions give a halogen if concentrated enough. Otherwise OH⁻ is discharged and oxygen forms. Sulfate and nitrate are not discharged.

flashcards.front: Products of electrolysing brine
flashcards.back: Hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, and sodium hydroxide solution is left.

flashcards.front: Why is cryolite used in aluminium extraction?
flashcards.back: It dissolves aluminium oxide and lowers the melting temperature, which saves a lot of energy.

flashcards.front: Ratio of gas volumes from electrolysing water
flashcards.back: Hydrogen : oxygen is 2 : 1 by volume, from 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂.

subject: chemistry

questions.content: Electroplating is used on cheap metal objects such as cutlery. What does electroplating do?
options: Coats an object with a thin layer of another metal using electrolysis
Melts an object so that it can be reshaped
Removes the outer layer of an object
Joins two metals using a flame
questions.explanation: Electroplating deposits a thin layer of a metal onto an object using an electric current.

questions.content: A key is to be plated with copper. Which electrode should the key be?
options: The anode, connected to the positive terminal
The cathode, connected to the negative terminal
Either electrode
It should not be connected to the power supply
questions.explanation: Metal ions are positive and are deposited at the cathode, so the object to be plated is the cathode.

questions.content: Which is a common reason for electroplating iron objects with chromium or zinc?
options: To make the iron heavier
To protect the iron from rusting and improve its appearance
To make the iron magnetic
To lower the melting point of the iron
questions.explanation: A plated layer shields iron from air and water and can give a shiny, attractive finish.

questions.content: A student plates a spoon with copper. Which solution should be used as the electrolyte?
options: Sodium chloride solution
Copper(II) sulfate solution
Distilled water
Dilute hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: The electrolyte must contain ions of the plating metal, so copper(II) sulfate solution supplies Cu²⁺ ions.

questions.content: In the set-up for copper plating, which material is the best choice for the anode?
options: A graphite rod
A piece of copper
A piece of plastic
A platinum wire
questions.explanation: A copper anode dissolves to replace the Cu²⁺ ions that are removed at the cathode, keeping the solution's concentration steady.

questions.content: Impure copper is refined by electrolysis. Which set-up is correct?
options: Impure copper as the cathode and pure copper as the anode
Impure copper as the anode and pure copper as the cathode
Both electrodes made of impure copper
Both electrodes made of graphite
questions.explanation: Copper dissolves from the impure anode and is deposited as pure copper on the cathode. Unwanted impurities fall to the bottom as sludge.

questions.content: During copper plating with a copper anode, the blue colour of the copper(II) sulfate solution stays about the same. Why?
options: No copper ions are discharged
Copper dissolving at the anode replaces the copper ions deposited at the cathode
Water is replacing the copper ions
The sulfate ions are turning into copper
questions.explanation: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the anode happens at about the same rate as Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu at the cathode, so the concentration stays constant.

questions.content: A student weighs a cathode before and after copper plating. Before: 12.40 g. After: 13.04 g. What mass of copper was deposited?
questions.explanation: Mass deposited = 13.04 − 12.40 = 0.64 g. Remember to subtract the starting mass from the final mass.

questions.content: Which half-equation describes what happens at the cathode when a spoon is silver plated?
options: Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻
Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag
Ag⁺ → Ag + e⁻
2Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag₂
questions.explanation: Silver ions each gain one electron to become a silver atom. This is reduction at the cathode.

questions.content: Which pairing of product and use from the electrolysis of brine is correct?
options: Chlorine, used to disinfect water
Sodium hydroxide, used to make fuel for cars
Hydrogen, used to bleach paper
Chlorine, used to make soap from sodium hydroxide
questions.explanation: Chlorine kills bacteria in drinking water and swimming pools. Sodium hydroxide is used to make soap and paper, and hydrogen is used in margarine manufacture and as a fuel.

questions.content: Aluminium objects can be anodised. What is the purpose of this process?
options: To thicken the natural oxide layer so the metal resists corrosion
To coat the metal with copper
To remove oxygen from the aluminium
To make the metal conduct better
questions.explanation: In anodising the aluminium is the anode. Oxygen formed there thickens the oxide layer, which is hard and protective and can also be dyed.

questions.content: A student plates a coin and finds that 0.32 g of metal is deposited in 10 minutes. Everything is kept the same except the time, which is doubled. Assuming a constant current, what mass is predicted?
questions.explanation: At a constant current, mass deposited is proportional to time. Doubling the time doubles the mass to 0.64 g.

questions.content: A jeweller plates a cheap metal ring with a thin layer of gold rather than making the ring from solid gold. Which is the best justification?
options: Gold plating makes the ring much stronger than solid gold
It gives the appearance and tarnish resistance of gold at a much lower cost
Solid gold cannot conduct electricity
Gold plating makes the ring lighter than any other metal
questions.explanation: Only a very thin layer of the expensive metal is needed on the surface, so the cost drops a lot. Plating does not make the ring stronger than solid gold.

questions.content: In a plating experiment, the cathode gains 0.64 g and the copper anode loses 0.66 g. Which is the most reasonable comment?
options: The 0.02 g difference could come from tiny pieces of copper flaking off the anode or from measurement error
The results prove that electrolysis creates mass
The results prove the cathode must have been weighed wet
The anode must be a different metal
questions.explanation: A difference this small is likely due to flaking, incomplete drying or the precision of the balance. Electrolysis does not create or destroy mass.

questions.content: A student connects a steel spoon to the positive terminal and a silver rod to the negative terminal in silver nitrate solution. What is most likely to happen?
options: The spoon is plated with silver as planned
The spoon dissolves slightly and the silver rod is plated
Nothing happens because the electrodes are different metals
Hydrogen gas is made at the spoon only
questions.explanation: The spoon is the anode, where metal atoms lose electrons and dissolve. Silver ions are discharged at the silver rod, which is the cathode, so the plan is reversed.

questions.content: A plater deposits 0.32 g of copper in 10 minutes at a steady current and wants to deposit 0.80 g using the same set-up. Which time is needed, and which assumption does the prediction rely on?
options: 25 minutes; the current stays constant
32 minutes; the current stays constant
25 minutes; the voltage is irrelevant and the current can vary freely
8 minutes; the current is doubled
questions.explanation: 0.32 g per 10 minutes is 0.032 g per minute, and 0.80 ÷ 0.032 = 25 minutes. This only works if the current is constant, because the deposited mass depends on the charge passed.

questions.content: Which statement correctly compares copper plating a key with refining impure copper?
options: In both, the copper anode dissolves and copper is deposited on the cathode
In plating the electrolyte contains no metal ions, but in refining it does
In refining, the cathode is the impure copper
Only plating uses a copper(II) sulfate solution
questions.explanation: In both processes copper dissolves from the anode and Cu²⁺ ions are discharged as copper at the cathode. The difference is the purpose and the nature of the cathode: a key versus a pure copper sheet.

questions.content: A factory has an electroplating line. Its waste water contains dissolved nickel ions. Which response best shows an understanding of sustainability?
options: Pour it into the river because the amount is small
Remove the nickel ions, for example by precipitation, and recycle the metal before releasing treated water
Boil it until it disappears
Dilute it with extra water until the smell is gone
questions.explanation: Heavy metal ions are toxic to living things and do not break down. Removing and recycling them protects the environment and saves resources. Dilution only spreads the pollution.

note:
## Electroplating
Electroplating is the use of electrolysis to coat an object with a thin layer of metal. It is done for three main reasons: to **protect** a metal from corrosion (for example zinc or chromium on iron), to improve **appearance** (silver or gold on cheaper metals), and sometimes to improve **hardness** or wear resistance.

## The set-up
The same simple rules apply every time.
- The **object to be plated** is the **cathode** (connected to the negative terminal).
- The **anode** is a piece of the **plating metal**, for example copper.
- The **electrolyte** is a solution containing ions of the plating metal, for example copper(II) sulfate.

At the cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. At the anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. Copper dissolves from the anode at about the same rate as it is deposited on the cathode, so the electrolyte stays blue and its concentration stays almost constant.

## Factors that affect the layer
The mass of metal deposited depends on the **current** and on the **time**. If the current is constant, doubling the time doubles the mass. For example, 0.32 g in 10 minutes means 0.032 g per minute, so 0.80 g would need 0.80 ÷ 0.032 = 25 minutes. This only works if the current stays steady. The object should also be clean and grease-free so the layer sticks properly.

## Refining copper
Copper from smelting is impure, but electrical wires need very pure copper because impurities increase resistance. In refining, a thick block of **impure copper is the anode** and a thin sheet of **pure copper is the cathode** in copper(II) sulfate solution. Copper dissolves from the anode and pure copper builds up on the cathode. Unreactive impurities such as silver and gold fall off as **anode sludge**, which can be collected and sold.

## Other uses of electrolysis
- **Extracting reactive metals** such as aluminium, sodium and potassium, which cannot be obtained by heating with carbon.
- **Chlor-alkali industry**: electrolysis of brine makes chlorine (disinfecting water, making bleach and plastics such as PVC), sodium hydroxide (soap, paper, cleaning products) and hydrogen (margarine, fuel).
- **Anodising aluminium**: aluminium is made the anode in dilute acid so the natural oxide layer becomes thicker, harder and more resistant to corrosion. The layer can also be dyed.

## Worked example
A cathode has a mass of 12.40 g before plating and 13.04 g after. Mass of copper deposited = 13.04 − 12.40 = 0.64 g. If the anode lost 0.66 g, the small difference could be due to bits flaking off or to the balance's limits, not to a real change in mass.

## Common mistakes
- Making the object the anode. It would then dissolve rather than be plated.
- Using an electrolyte that does not contain the plating metal's ions.
- Saying that the current is used up. Charge is carried round the circuit; it is not used up.
- Forgetting to subtract the starting mass when working out the mass deposited.

## Environmental and economic issues
Electroplating and metal extraction use a lot of electrical energy, and waste solutions can contain toxic metal ions such as nickel or chromium. A responsible plant treats and recycles its waste and uses renewable energy where possible.

## How this is examined
Questions often give a context such as a factory plating car parts or a refinery producing wire. You may be asked to state which electrode is which, calculate the mass deposited, predict how changing time or current changes the result, and evaluate sources of error and the environmental impact.

Exam tip: State clearly that the object is the cathode, name the electrolyte ion, and write the half-equation with electrons on the correct side.

flashcards.back: Using electrolysis to coat an object with a thin layer of metal, for protection, appearance or wear resistance.

flashcards.front: Which electrode is the object being plated?
flashcards.back: The cathode (negative), because the positive metal ions are deposited there.

flashcards.front: What should the anode be in electroplating?
flashcards.back: A piece of the plating metal, which dissolves to replace the ions that are used up.

flashcards.front: What should the electrolyte contain?
flashcards.back: Ions of the plating metal, for example copper(II) sulfate solution for copper plating.

flashcards.front: Half-equation at the cathode in copper plating
flashcards.back: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

flashcards.front: How is impure copper refined?
flashcards.back: Impure copper is the anode and pure copper the cathode in copper(II) sulfate solution. Impurities fall away as sludge.

flashcards.front: What factors change the mass of metal deposited?
flashcards.back: The current and the time. At constant current, the mass deposited is proportional to time.

flashcards.front: Name three uses of products from brine electrolysis
flashcards.back: Chlorine disinfects water and makes bleach, sodium hydroxide makes soap and paper, hydrogen is used in margarine and as a fuel.

flashcards.front: What is anodising?
flashcards.back: Making aluminium the anode in dilute acid so its natural oxide layer becomes thicker, harder and more corrosion resistant.

subject: chemistry

questions.content: A student builds a simple cell. Which items are needed?
options: Two different metals and an electrolyte
Two identical metals and distilled water
One metal and a dry powder
Two non-metals and an acid
questions.explanation: A simple cell needs two different metals as electrodes dipping into an electrolyte, joined by a wire.

questions.content: A simple cell uses copper as one electrode. Which second electrode would give the largest voltage?
options: Magnesium
Zinc
Iron
Silver
questions.explanation: The greater the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the greater the voltage. Magnesium is the furthest from copper in reactivity among these.

questions.content: In a simple cell made from zinc and copper, which metal is the negative terminal?
options: Copper, because it is less reactive
Zinc, because it is more reactive
Both are negative
Neither, because the electrolyte is negative
questions.explanation: The more reactive metal loses electrons more readily, so zinc becomes the negative terminal and electrons flow from it through the wire.

questions.content: In which direction do electrons flow in the external wire of a zinc-copper cell?
options: From copper to zinc
From zinc to copper
Through the electrolyte from zinc to copper
They do not flow
questions.explanation: Electrons flow through the wire from the more reactive metal (zinc) to the less reactive metal (copper). In the electrolyte, ions carry the charge.

questions.content: What is the main difference between a rechargeable battery and a non-rechargeable battery?
options: Rechargeable batteries contain no chemicals
A rechargeable battery's reaction can be reversed by passing a current through it
Non-rechargeable batteries always give a higher voltage
Rechargeable batteries only work once
questions.explanation: In a rechargeable cell, electrical energy applied during charging reverses the chemical reaction. In a non-rechargeable cell the reaction cannot be easily reversed.

questions.content: A student measures the voltage of cells that all use a copper electrode paired with another metal. The readings are: magnesium 2.0 V, zinc 1.0 V, iron 0.7 V, lead 0.5 V. Which is the correct order of reactivity from most to least reactive?
options: Lead, iron, zinc, magnesium
Magnesium, zinc, iron, lead
Zinc, magnesium, lead, iron
Magnesium, iron, zinc, lead
questions.explanation: A larger voltage with copper shows the metal is further from copper in reactivity, so it is more reactive. The voltage order is Mg > Zn > Fe > Pb.

questions.content: Which half-equation shows what happens at the zinc electrode in a zinc-copper cell?
options: Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn
Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
Zn → Zn²⁺ + e⁻
Zn + 2e⁻ → Zn²⁺
questions.explanation: Zinc atoms lose two electrons to become zinc ions. This is oxidation, and the electrons leave through the external wire.

questions.content: A student sets up a cell with two identical copper strips in copper sulfate solution. The voltmeter reads 0 V. What is the best explanation?
options: Copper sulfate is not an electrolyte
There is no difference in reactivity between the electrodes
The wires are too long
Copper is not a conductor
questions.explanation: A cell needs two different metals to create a difference in the tendency to lose electrons. Identical electrodes give no potential difference.

questions.content: A simple cell gradually produces less voltage and eventually stops. What is the main reason?
options: The electrons are used up
The reactants are being used up
The wire gets longer
The electrolyte becomes a solid
questions.explanation: The cell runs on a chemical reaction. When the more reactive metal or ions have been used up, the reaction slows down and the cell goes flat. Electrons are not used up; they flow around the circuit.

questions.content: A hydrogen fuel cell combines hydrogen and oxygen. Which is the overall equation, and what is the only product?
options: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O; water
H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂; hydrogen peroxide
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O; carbon dioxide and water
H₂ + O → H₂O; steam and soot
questions.explanation: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form only water. The equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O is balanced.

questions.content: Which statement describes a key difference between a fuel cell and a rechargeable battery?
options: A fuel cell needs a continuous supply of fuel, whereas a battery has a limited store of chemicals
A fuel cell must be recharged using mains electricity
A battery produces no electricity
A fuel cell contains no electrolyte
questions.explanation: A fuel cell keeps working as long as fuel and oxygen are supplied. A battery has a fixed amount of reactants and must be recharged.

questions.content: In a simple cell, why is an electrolyte solution used instead of pure water?
options: Ions in the electrolyte carry charge through the solution and complete the circuit
Pure water is too cold
Electrolytes cause the metals to join together
Pure water would be oxidised to hydrogen
questions.explanation: Pure water has almost no ions. A dissolved salt or acid supplies ions that move between the electrodes, so the circuit is complete.

questions.content: A student builds a cell with a zinc electrode and a copper electrode, both dipping in aqueous copper(II) sulfate, and connects them with a wire. What happens at the copper electrode?
options: Copper ions gain electrons and copper metal is deposited
Copper atoms lose electrons and the electrode dissolves
Zinc ions gain electrons and zinc is deposited
Hydrogen ions gain electrons and hydrogen gas is made
questions.explanation: Zinc is more reactive, so it is the negative electrode and sends electrons along the wire. At the copper electrode Cu²⁺ ions pick up these electrons (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu), which is reduction.

questions.content: In a hydrogen fuel cell, 4 g of hydrogen reacts completely with oxygen. The relative atomic masses are H = 1 and O = 16. What mass of oxygen is needed, and what mass of water is made?
options: 32 g of oxygen; 36 g of water
16 g of oxygen; 20 g of water
64 g of oxygen; 68 g of water
32 g of oxygen; 28 g of water
questions.explanation: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 4 g of H₂ is 2 mol, which needs 1 mol of O₂ (32 g). The water mass is 4 + 32 = 36 g, by conservation of mass.

questions.content: A student pairs each of two unknown metals with copper. Metal X gives 0.5 V and metal Y gives 1.3 V, and in both cases X and Y are the negative terminals. If X and Y are joined in a cell, which prediction is best?
options: Y is the negative terminal and the voltage is about 0.8 V
X is the negative terminal and the voltage is about 0.8 V
Y is the negative terminal and the voltage is about 1.8 V
The voltage is 0 V
questions.explanation: Y is further from copper in reactivity than X, so it is more reactive and is the negative terminal against X. The voltage is roughly the difference, 1.3 − 0.5 = 0.8 V.

questions.content: A newspaper says: "Hydrogen cars have zero environmental impact." Which is the best evaluation of the claim?
options: Correct, because hydrogen can never be harmful
Partly true: the car only emits water, but making the hydrogen can use fossil fuels and produce carbon dioxide
False, because hydrogen cars emit large amounts of carbon dioxide at the exhaust
False, because water is a pollutant
questions.explanation: At the point of use the only product is water, but a full evaluation includes how the hydrogen is produced and stored. If it is made using fossil fuel energy, emissions are only moved elsewhere.

questions.content: A rechargeable battery is being charged. Which statement about the chemistry is correct?
options: Electrical energy drives the reaction in the reverse direction, restoring the original reactants
The battery makes more chemicals from nothing
The electrons are poured back into the metal as a liquid
The chemical reaction stops completely
questions.explanation: During charging, the power supply forces a current in the opposite direction, so the products of discharge are converted back to reactants. Energy is stored as chemical energy.

questions.content: A cell has a magnesium and a copper electrode in salt solution and initially gives 2.0 V. After 30 minutes it gives 0.2 V. Which of the following is the best evidence-based conclusion?
options: The magnesium has been partly consumed and the reaction has slowed, though other factors such as a build-up of products on the electrodes could also contribute
Copper has become more reactive than magnesium
The voltmeter must be broken because voltages never change
The salt solution has changed into pure water
questions.explanation: Reactants are used up over time and products can coat the electrodes, both reducing the voltage. Metals do not change their position in the reactivity series, and voltage does fall as cells discharge.

note:
## How a simple cell works
A **cell** converts chemical energy into electrical energy. A simple cell has two electrodes made from **different metals**, dipping into an **electrolyte** (a solution containing ions). The electrodes are connected by a wire, and the electrolyte completes the circuit.

The more reactive metal has a greater tendency to lose electrons, so it becomes the **negative terminal**. For a zinc-copper cell:
- At the zinc electrode: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation). The zinc slowly dissolves.
- Electrons travel through the external wire from zinc to copper.
- At the copper electrode: positive ions in the electrolyte, such as Cu²⁺ or H⁺, gain the electrons (reduction).
- In the electrolyte, ions carry the charge, so the circuit is complete.

Electrons never travel through the electrolyte; the ions do that job.

## What affects the voltage?
The **voltage** depends mainly on the pair of metals. The further apart the two metals are in the reactivity series, the larger the voltage. A magnesium-copper cell gives a larger voltage than a zinc-copper cell, and a cell with two identical electrodes gives 0 V.

You can use voltage data to rank metals. If metals are each paired with copper and give readings of 2.0 V (magnesium), 1.0 V (zinc), 0.7 V (iron) and 0.5 V (lead), then the order of reactivity is magnesium > zinc > iron > lead. If two unknown metals give 0.5 V and 1.3 V against copper, then a cell made from the two of them gives about 1.3 − 0.5 = 0.8 V, with the 1.3 V metal as the negative terminal.

## Why cells go flat
A cell stops when the reactants are used up, so the voltage falls over time. Products building up on electrodes can also reduce the voltage. Electrons are not used up; they keep flowing round the circuit while the reaction continues.

## Batteries
A **battery** is two or more cells joined together, which gives a higher voltage.
- **Non-rechargeable (primary)** batteries, such as many alkaline batteries, cannot easily be reversed. They are thrown away or recycled when flat.
- **Rechargeable (secondary)** batteries, such as lithium-ion, can be recharged because passing a current in the opposite direction reverses the reaction and restores the reactants. They can be used hundreds of times.

## Fuel cells
A **hydrogen fuel cell** reacts hydrogen with oxygen from air: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. It makes electricity directly and the only product is water. It keeps working as long as fuel is supplied, unlike a battery that holds a fixed store of chemicals.

Worked example: 4 g of hydrogen is 2 mol. It needs 1 mol of oxygen, which is 32 g, and makes 36 g of water. Mass is conserved: 4 + 32 = 36.

## Advantages and disadvantages
- Fuel cells: only water at the point of use, quiet and efficient; but hydrogen is hard to store and may be made using fossil fuels.
- Rechargeable batteries: can be reused many times; but they need mining of materials, have limited lifespan and must be recycled safely.

## Common mistakes
- Saying electrons move through the electrolyte.
- Assuming the less reactive metal is the negative terminal.
- Saying that a flat cell has "run out of electrons".
- Calling the fuel cell "pollution free" without thinking about how the hydrogen is made.

## How this is examined
Questions often present a table of voltages from an investigation, ask you to rank metals, identify the negative terminal, draw conclusions about accuracy and then compare cells for a real situation such as powering a vehicle. Sustainability arguments should consider the whole life cycle of the technology.

Exam tip: When ranking metals from cell voltages, say that a bigger voltage with the same reference metal means the metal is more reactive.

flashcards.front: What is needed to make a simple cell?
flashcards.back: Two different metals as electrodes, an electrolyte, and a wire joining the electrodes.

flashcards.front: Which electrode is the negative terminal?
flashcards.back: The more reactive metal, because it loses electrons more readily and electrons flow from it.

flashcards.front: Direction of electron flow in a simple cell
flashcards.back: Through the external wire from the more reactive metal to the less reactive metal.

flashcards.front: What decides the voltage of a simple cell?
flashcards.back: The difference in reactivity of the two metals. The greater the difference, the greater the voltage.

flashcards.front: Why does a cell go flat?
flashcards.back: The reactants are used up so the reaction slows and stops. Electrons are not used up.

flashcards.front: Define a battery.
flashcards.back: Two or more cells connected together to give a higher voltage.

flashcards.front: How does a rechargeable battery work?
flashcards.back: A current is passed through in the reverse direction, which reverses the reaction and restores the reactants.

flashcards.front: Hydrogen fuel cell equation
flashcards.back: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Water is the only product at the point of use.

flashcards.front: Fuel cell compared with a battery
flashcards.back: A fuel cell works continuously while fuel is supplied; a battery contains a fixed amount of chemicals and goes flat.
